claim: Boroditsky 2001 Mandarin vertical-time priming effect (54 ms mean bias, N=20 Mandarin) was reported once with small samples; later attempts (Chen 2007; January and Kako 2007, six experiments on English monolinguals; Tse and Altarriba 2008) did not reproduce it cleanly. Tse and Altarriba partly replicated the bilingual half, but English and bilingual groups both showed a vertical-prime advantage. Per-study N and effect sizes were not recovered.
agent_test: Only background: do not build on it. Exact Ns for the failed replications are still unread.

claim: Space-time asymmetry (space distorts time estimates more than time distorts space) holds across Dutch, Brazilian adults and children, and is consistent with metaphor-use frequency (Casasanto 2010; Bottini and Casasanto 2013).
agent_test: Test whether an LLM's duration estimates are shifted by irrelevant length cues more than length estimates are shifted by duration cues, at equal tokens.

claim: Pitch metaphor differs by language (Dutch height, Farsi/Turkish thickness) and the difference shows in nonlinguistic psychophysics tasks; 2-hour thickness training moves Dutch speakers toward Farsi (Dolscheid 2013, 2020).
agent_test: Prompt an LLM with height vs thickness pitch metaphor wording and measure matching bias in a non-verbal-style pairing task.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-20 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Pitch-height association is not purely linguistic: infants of 3-4 months prefer height-pitch congruence, and thickness-pitch is shared by both Dutch and Turkish groups; language modulates rather than creates the mapping.
agent_test: Check whether weakening the verbal cue in an LLM prompt removes the bias or leaves a residual.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-20 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Reading and writing direction (not spoken metaphor) drives horizontal time layout; mirror reading reverses past-left mapping (87.5% vs a mirror baseline whose exact value is unresolved (46.9% or 53.1%, complement of each other) and 78.1% vs 40.6%), and writing-only manipulations did not (Casasanto and Bottini 2014; Crossley and Bylund 2025).
agent_test: Not directly testable on an LLM; note that token order, not meaning, may carry the analogous bias.

claim: Mandarin vertical-time bias depends on region and reading habit: found in Taiwan, not China, and explained by vertical text experience, not by the spoken metaphor alone.
agent_test: None.

claim: Mandarin and English bilinguals' time-axis use depends on current-language context and immediate cues (Lai and Boroditsky 2013: ego-moving answer 68.2% English, 38.2% bilinguals, 0% Mandarin); the effect is partly an online language-use effect.
agent_test: Ask the same time-ambiguity question in different prompt languages and compare answer rates.

claim: Absolute-frame languages (Pormpuraaw) lay out time east-to-west independent of body, but samples are tiny (N=9 in Fedden and Boroditsky), and the Tsimane' show only 42% same-direction across three magnitude domains, so a universal mapping is not supported.
agent_test: None.

claim: Russian blues (Winawer 2007) category effect failed to replicate in a direct replication (Martinovic 2020, no boundary effect, p=.29), and appears only when the boundary is shifted by trial frequency context.
agent_test: Use only as caution against over-reading category-perception results.

claim: LLMs encode spatial and temporal coordinates linearly (R2 about 0.91 world, 0.75 headlines for Llama-2-70b at 60% depth); this is a representational fact, not evidence of Whorfian effects.
agent_test: Probe our agent's model for time/place directions before building any spatial scratchpad; low value as prompt design.

claim: LLM reasoning accuracy differs by prompt language in a small bilingual causal-order test (Wang 2025, 400 samples): second table Qwen1.5-1.8B En 88.5 vs Zh 76.8 and Mistral-7B 93.8 vs 81.5, but Qwen1.5-14B 97.5 vs 97.5, 32B 90.5 vs 94.0, 72B 97.0 vs 96.2. The gap shrinks with scale inside Qwen, appears in Mistral-7B, and a language effect cannot be separated from a data-mix effect because no control was run. Table 1 (plain accuracy) shows Llama-3.2-3B Chinese 56.8 vs English 27.0.
agent_test: Run forward and reversed causal prompts in two languages on our model at the working size; do not assume language neutrality below about 7B.

claim: LLM answers on temporal discounting differ by language future-time reference (Goli and Singh 2024): larger-later chosen 22% GPT-3.5, 16% GPT-4, 34.5% GPT-4 with chain of thought; weak vs strong FTR confidence intervals touch at 1.948 in standard conjoint. No independent replication of the LLM effect was found, and the human mechanism it rests on failed a direct test: in English speakers more habitual future-tense use predicted less discounting (PLOS ONE 2025, N=235 and N=606).
agent_test: Re-run in our agent language prompts; the strong-vs-weak FTR difference is only marginal so treat as null until replicated.

claim: LLM sound-shape and iconicity effects are weaker than human ones: CLIP 52% and Stable Diffusion 80% on kiki-bouba vs humans 89%; GPT-4 iconicity rating Spearman about .54 to .58.
agent_test: Background only.

claim: Vision-language and LLM spatial frame-of-reference reasoning is weak and prompt-dependent: VLM aggregate 47-63% under explicit frame prompts; best conversion 55.5%; humans above 90%.
agent_test: Test whether stating the reference frame explicitly in the prompt raises accuracy at equal tokens (Spatial-Guided prompting reported gains).

claim: No study found that directly tests whether ego-moving vs time-moving framing, spatial-metaphor wording, or the space-time distance-duration asymmetry changes an LLM's non-linguistic task behaviour (about 20 more searches this pass, 0 hits). Nearest items: deictic vs sequential time frame (Zhang and Rayz 2026), vocabulary-constraint agents (Jehu-Appiah 2026), Yoruba prompting (n=10).
agent_test: Design a small prompt-framing test: ambiguous 'move meeting forward' questions across wording frames.

claim: Gender-grammar neo-Whorfian effects are not supported by distributional embeddings once noun meaning is controlled (Kann 2019, Stanczak 2023), so grammatical categories alone do not produce the reported effect.
agent_test: None; confirms that surface wording alone is a weak lever.

claim: Language effects on LLM pitch judgements are untested: GPT-4 predicts human pitch similarity at r=.92 (N=55 humans, English prompts only) and recovers octave equivalence, but no study varies height vs thickness metaphor wording or prompt language for pitch.
agent_test: Prompt a model with high/low vs thick/thin wording on pitch-order tasks.

claim: LLM colour naming depends on prompt language: GPT-4 adjusted Rand index vs humans 0.59 English and 0.54 Russian (lab ceiling about 0.73-0.75), with different partitions from the same hex codes. This is a naming-vocabulary effect; no study tests the Winawer discrimination (speed) advantage on a model.
agent_test: Background only.

claim: Cross-language LLM colour differences are partly lexicon artifacts: spelling-based scoring explains 0-5% of the alignment score in English and Spanish and 32-71% in Chinese (r=0.84 with the share of self-naming terms); on matched 43 colours four languages are not separable. Multilingual layers share colour-language geometry early (congruence 0.61-0.71) and diverge late (0.29-0.56).
agent_test: Any language-as-variable LLM test needs vocabulary controls.

claim: Imposed vocabulary or prompt-language changes alter LLM outputs but mostly through topic, verbosity and model-specific effects: Yoruba prompting n=10 SGI 0.795 vs 0.128 (preprint); No-Have +19.1 pp on ethical reasoning, E-Prime -27.5 pp to +42.3 pp by model (N=4,470 trials, preprint, no length-matched control). A diverse 3-agent ensemble reached 100% vs 88.2% coverage on 17 debugging problems.
agent_test: Test linguistic-constraint diversity as one ensemble member lever, with a length-matched control.

claim: Casasanto (2016) frames linguistic, cultural and bodily relativity as one mechanism: experience strengthens some implicit associations and weakens others, so language is not special. Only the abstract was read; the Routledge chapter is unread.
agent_test: Treat wording effects as habit-strengthened associations.

claim: Mandarin-English bilinguals can hold both horizontal and vertical timelines and switch with cultural context cues (Miles et al. 2011: bilinguals 736 ms compatible vs 772 ms incompatible in both orientations; Chinese actor photos pushed vertical ordering).
agent_test: Frame choice can be triggered by cheap context cues.

claim: Zhang and Rayz 2026 show frame-dependent, past-future asymmetric time judgements in Qwen3-4B and 30B under deictic framing (2.9M entries) but report no effect sizes and only English, so cross-language asymmetry is untested.
agent_test: State the time frame explicitly in prompts.
